section.title: Maximum Entropy
section.para:
To explain what maximum entropy is, it will be simplest to quote from Manning and Schütze* (p. 589):
Maximum entropy modeling is a framework for integrating information from many heterogeneous information sources for classification. The data for a classification problem is described as a (potentially large) number of features. These features can be quite complex and allow the experimenter to make use of prior knowledge about what types of information are expected to be important for classification. Each feature corresponds to a constraint on the model. We then compute the maximum entropy model, the model with the maximum entropy of all the models that satisfy the constraints. This term may seem perverse, since we have spent most of the book trying to minimize the (cross) entropy of models, but the idea is that we do not want to go beyond the data. If we chose a model with less entropy, we would add `information' constraints to the model that are not justified by the empirical evidence available to us. Choosing the maximum entropy model is motivated by the desire to preserve as much uncertainty as possible.
So that gives a rough idea of what the maximum entropy framework is. Don't assume anything about your probability distribution other than what you have observed.

On the engineering level, using maxent is an excellent way of creating programs which perform very difficult classification tasks very well. For example, precision and recall figures for programs using maxent models have reached (or are) the state of the art on tasks like part of speech tagging, sentence detection, prepositional phrase attachment, and named entity recognition. On the engineering level, an added benefit is that the person creating a maxent model only needs to inform the training procedure of the event space, and need not worry about independence between features.

While the authors of this implementation of maximum entropy are generally interested using maxent models in natural language processing, the framework is certainly quite general and useful for a much wider variety of fields. In fact, maximum entropy modeling was originally developed for statistical physics.

For a very in-depth discussion of how maxent can be used in natural language processing, try reading Adwait Ratnaparkhi's dissertation. Also, check out Berger, Della Pietra, and Della Pietra's paper A Maximum Entropy Approach to Natural Language Processing, which provides an excellent introduction and discussion of the framework.
*Foundations of statistical natural language processing. Christopher D. Manning, Hinrich Schütze. Cambridge, Mass.: MIT Press, c1999.

section.title: Implementation
section.para: We have tried to make the opennlp.maxent implementation easy to use. To create a model, one needs (of course) the training data, and then implementations of two interfaces in the opennlp.maxent package, EventStream and ContextGenerator. These have fairly simple specifications, and example implementations can be found in the OpenNLP Tools preprocessing components.

BasicContextGenerator turns one string of contextual predicates into the predicate array. Without arguments it separates on runs of whitespace under the Unicode White_Space property (StringUtil.isUnicodeWhitespace), independent of the opennlp.whitespace.mode setting. A separator given to the constructor is taken as written, not as a regular expression, and must not be null, empty, or contain an unpaired surrogate. A predicate is never empty: leading, repeated, or trailing separators produce none, and an empty input gives no predicates.

We have also set in place some interfaces and code to make it easier to automate the training and evaluation process (the Evaluable interface and the TrainEval class). It is not necessary to use this functionality, but if you do you'll find it much easier to see how well your models are doing. The opennlp.grok.preprocess.namefind package is an example of a maximum entropy component which uses this functionality.

Events with real-valued features can also be read from a text file, one event per line, through RealValueFileEventStream, or from any line stream through RealBasicEventStream. The fields of a line are separated by runs of Unicode whitespace, that is characters with the White_Space property such as a tab or a no-break space; this definition is fixed and does not depend on the opennlp.whitespace.mode property. Leading, trailing, and repeated whitespace is ignored. The first field is the outcome and each further field is a context, optionally followed by = and its real value. The value follows the last =, so a context name may contain that character; a context whose text after the last = is not a number is kept as written with the value 1, and an error is logged. A line with only an outcome is an event without contexts, and a blank line is reported as an InvalidFormatException. FileEventStream is unchanged: it reads events without values and splits on spaces, tabs, and form feeds only. An example with real values:
other wc=ic=1.0 w&c=he,ic=2.0 n1wc=lc=3.0 org-start wc=ic=1.0 w&c=apache,ic=2.0 p1wc=lc=3.0

We have managed to use several techniques to reduce the size of the models when writing them to disk, which also means that reading in a model for use is much quicker than with less compact encodings of the model. This was especially important to us since we use many maxent models in the Grok library, and we wanted the start up time and the physical size of the library to be as minimal as possible. As of version 1.2.0, maxent has an io package which greatly simplifies the process of loading and saving models in different formats.

section.title: Text embedding providers
section.para: TextEmbedder in opennlp-api accepts text and returns vectors. TextEmbedderProvider creates independently owned models. The API names no backend: opennlp-dl registers the onnx provider, and it is the default only because it is the one provider in the default distribution.

TextEmbedderProviders.select considers the installed providers that report themselves available (isAvailable, for example their runtime classes are present) and that support the request (supports, for example a model file named *.onnx with the provider's own options). The one with the highest priority wins, so a module can replace another module's provider by registering the same name with a larger priority. Two supporting providers with the same priority are reported as ambiguous. The system property opennlp.embedder.provider pins a provider by name and skips the capability check; TextEmbedderProviders.get("name") does the same in code. A missing provider fails with the names of the installed ones. Excluding opennlp-dl leaves the API without a provider until another one is installed.

Providers register their public, no-argument factory in META-INF/services/opennlp.tools.embeddings.TextEmbedderProvider. Factory construction and the availability check must not load models or initialize a native runtime. A registration that cannot be loaded is skipped with a warning, so one broken provider jar does not hide the others. Discovery uses the class path; OpenNLP ships no module descriptors, so a provider used from the module path needs its own provides clause. The ONNX provider requires vocabulary, resolved relative to the model's parent directory, and accepts lowerCase=true (default) or lowerCase=false. Unknown options are rejected. Existing SentenceVectorsDL constructors remain available.
